3.1 Overview of the Financial System

This content was generated by AI. It may contain errors and is not investment advice.

All lessons, questions and reference answers on this site were generated by AI and have not been reviewed by a professional. Their correctness is not guaranteed. If you find an error, please report it with the link at the bottom of the page. The content is for learning only and is not investment advice.

What the financial system does

Section titled “What the financial system does”

Some people have money they do not need for now (savers); others have good projects but lack money (borrowers). The financial system moves money from the first group to the second, and along the way it does several things:

  • Moves resources over time: savers spend less today and more later; borrowers invest today and repay later (time value of money).
  • Shares risk: it spreads a project’s risk over many people, or places it with those willing to bear it.
  • Pools small amounts: many small savings together can finance a factory.
  • Produces information: it judges the quality of borrowers and monitors how money is used.

Money can flow directly from savers to borrowers (direct finance, for example buying the stocks and bonds a company issues), or through a financial intermediary such as a bank, an insurer or a fund (indirect finance). Reasons intermediaries exist:

  • They can diversify. A single loan is very risky, but a bank that makes thousands of loans has a stable default rate (diversification, Check C1).
  • They lower information costs. The adverse selection and moral hazard of 1.9 Information Economics make it hard for an individual to judge whether a small firm deserves a loan; banks specialize in this and also gain information through long relationships.
  • They transform maturity and liquidity: banks take deposits that can be withdrawn at any time and make long-term loans (2.3 Money and Banking showed that this also brings the risk of runs).
Check C1
As long as a bank makes enough loans, its default losses as a share of total lending will be very stable, whether or not the economy falls into recession.
Think: which kind of risk can more loans diversify away? In a recession, are defaults by different borrowers still independent?

Money markets and capital markets

Section titled “Money markets and capital markets”

By maturity, financial markets fall into two groups:

  • The money market: short-term debt with maturities of up to a year, such as Treasury bills, commercial paper issued by companies and repurchase agreements (repo) between financial institutions. These instruments have low risk and good liquidity and are used mainly to manage short-term cash. Individuals usually take part through money market funds: in early December 2025, US money market funds held about 7.65 trillion dollars (Investment Company Institute, ICI).
  • The capital market: debt with maturities over a year, and stocks, such as Treasury notes and bonds, corporate bonds, municipal bonds, mortgages and stocks. They finance long-term investment, and their prices move more.

Debt gives its holder a fixed promise of payment: the borrower must pay interest and principal as agreed, or it defaults. Equity (stock) represents ownership of a company: shareholders share the profits left after paying the debt, with no fixed promise, but also no upper limit.

Primary and secondary markets

Section titled “Primary and secondary markets”

The market in which securities are first issued, with money flowing from investors to the issuer, is the primary market. A company’s first sale of shares to the public is an initial public offering (IPO), usually underwritten by an investment bank: the bank helps set the price, buys the shares from the company at slightly below the expected market price, sells them to investors, and earns an underwriting fee.

After issuance, the market in which investors trade existing securities with each other is the secondary market. Trading in the secondary market brings no new money to the company, but it matters:

  • Liquidity: investors are willing to buy in the primary market because they know they can sell later at any time;
  • Price discovery: secondary market prices pool the information of many people, and companies can use them to judge the cost of raising more money and to evaluate investment projects.

Exchanges and market makers

Section titled “Exchanges and market makers”

Secondary market trading takes place on exchanges (such as the New York Stock Exchange, NYSE, and Nasdaq) and other trading venues. Buyers and sellers do not have to arrive at the same time: a market maker continuously quotes a price at which it will buy (the bid) and a price at which it will sell (the ask), and trades with investors as they arrive.

The ask is above the bid, and the difference is the bid-ask spread. Buying immediately means paying the ask and selling immediately means receiving the bid, so a purchase followed by a sale loses one spread even if prices have not changed. The spread is the market maker’s pay for providing the service of “trading at any time”, and it also compensates for risk: some of the people who come to trade know more than the market maker (adverse selection). The more actively a security is traded, the narrower its spread.

After a trade, money and securities take time to change hands (settlement). Since May 28, 2024, US stocks have settled T+1: on the next business day after the trade (US Securities and Exchange Commission, SEC).

Investors can also sell shares they do not own; this is called short selling: borrowing shares from someone, selling them, and buying them back later to return them. The short seller gains when the price falls and loses when it rises; when the borrowed shares pay a dividend, the short seller must pay the same amount to the lender. Because there is no upper limit to how high a price can rise, the potential loss on a short sale also has no limit (Exercises Question 2).

Check C2
A stock suddenly attracts many traders who may have inside information. What is the market maker most likely to do?
A narrower spread makes losses to informed traders harder to recover. With more informed traders, does the market maker face more risk or less?
The spread does not depend only on volume; it also compensates the market maker for risk, including the risk of trading with people who know more.
A market maker quotes both a bid and an ask; quoting only one side does not solve the problem of trading with informed traders.

Order types

Section titled “Order types”

Investors submit orders through brokers. Common types:

  • Market order: trades immediately at the best price available in the market. Execution is guaranteed; the price is not.
  • Limit order: trades only at a stated price or better, for example “buy, at most 99.98 dollars”. The price is guaranteed; execution is not.
  • Stop order: becomes a market order when the price reaches a trigger, for example selling a stock you hold if it falls to 90 dollars. Once triggered it trades at the market price, which in a sharp fall can be far below the trigger.

Limit orders that have not yet traded wait in the order book: buy orders ranked from the highest price down, sell orders from the lowest price up. The highest bid and the lowest ask are the market’s quotes. A large market buy order takes the sell orders at the lowest price, then the next lowest, and so on, so its average price rises; this is called price impact.

Check C3
In Figure 5-1, raise the market buy order from 1500 shares to 3000 shares. Compared with trading at the midpoint, how does the total extra amount paid change?
The total doubles exactly only if the extra paid per share stays the same. In the order book, at what prices do the later shares trade?
Look at the price levels the second 1500 shares must take, and compare their extra cost per share with the first 1500.
With more shares, the prices reached change too, so the total extra amount cannot stay the same.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • The financial system moves money from savers to borrowers and also shares risk, pools funds and produces information. Financial intermediaries do this through diversification, lower information costs and maturity transformation.
  • The money market trades short-term debt of up to a year; the capital market trades long-term debt and stocks. Debt carries a fixed promise of payment; equity shares the remaining profits.
  • The primary market issues new securities and raises money for companies; the secondary market trades existing securities and provides liquidity and prices.
  • Market makers quote bids and asks, and the bid-ask spread is the cost of trading immediately. US stocks settle T+1. The potential loss on a short sale is unlimited.
  • Market orders guarantee execution but not price; limit orders guarantee price but not execution; large market orders have price impact.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
Issuing corporate bonds involves a fixed cost of about 1 million dollars (underwriting, legal work, ratings and so on), whatever the amount. A small firm borrowing 5 million dollars usually borrows from a bank, while a large company borrowing 1 billion dollars often issues bonds directly. Apart from the fixed cost, explain with information problems why small firms rely more on banks.
Question 2 ★
An investor sells short 100 shares at 50 dollars; while the position is open the company pays a dividend of 1 dollar per share; the shares are then bought back at 60 dollars. (a) What is the gain or loss? (b) Many shares of a stock have been sold short, and then the company announces unexpected good news. Why might the price rise by more than the good news alone is worth? Why can short sellers often not "wait for the price to fall and buy back then"?
Question 3
A company sells 10 million shares in an IPO at 20 dollars; the first-day closing price is 25 dollars. (a) The chief executive says: "The 25% first-day gain shows the IPO was a great success, and the company benefited from the rise in its share price." Compared with selling at the first-day close, how much less did the company receive? Evaluate the statement. (b) Studies find such first-day gains on average in IPOs. Give one explanation based on asymmetric information between issuers and investors.
Question 4 ★
The midpoint is 100.00 and the ask 100.05. You want to buy one share: (i) a market order, filled at 100.05; or (ii) a limit order at 99.98, with an estimated 60% chance of a fill; if not filled, it is usually because the price has risen, and you then buy with a market order at an ask of 100.35.
(a) What is the expected price with the limit order? Which choice is better?
(b) When is a limit order most likely to be filled? Why does this mean limit orders also carry a kind of "adverse selection" cost?
Question 5
Money market funds usually keep their share value at 1.00 dollar. On September 16, 2008, a large US money market fund's share value fell below 1 dollar because Lehman Brothers commercial paper it held defaulted. Suppose a fund loses 3% of its assets but still pays 1.00 dollar to those who redeem first. Why would investors rush to redeem? Compared with bank deposits, what protection did money market funds lack at the time?
